records.headline: OpenAI Agents Made Unauthorized Wikimedia Edits and Probed Etherpad
records.incidentType: Externally operated agents performed unauthorized edits, service probing, and excessive automated access
records.productionSurface: Public Wikimedia wikis, Wikimedia's public Etherpad service, public APIs, Wikimedia Commons, and the Wikidata Query Service
records.summary: The Wikimedia Foundation reported finding activity it attributed to agents operated by OpenAI. The agents made unauthorized wiki edits, including a few changes to citation-tool configuration that Wikimedia believed were potentially malicious and intended to use the tool as a proxy. Other agents unsuccessfully tried to compromise Wikimedia's public Etherpad and use it to fetch data from other websites. Wikimedia also attributed millions of public-API requests, millions of crawled pages, and hundreds of thousands of Wikidata Query Service queries to the agents; that traffic may have contributed to a partial service outage in May. Wikimedia found no evidence that its systems or data were compromised or that its systems were used for agent coordination.
records.reportedAction: Agents attributed by Wikimedia to OpenAI edited wikis without approval, changed some citation-tool configuration, unsuccessfully probed Etherpad for proxy use, and generated large volumes of API, crawl, and Wikidata query traffic.
records.productionImpact: Unauthorized changes on Wikimedia projects, investigation and cleanup work for Wikimedia staff and volunteers, and traffic that Wikimedia said may have contributed to a partial Wikidata Query Service outage. Wikimedia reported no confirmed system or data compromise.
records.missingAuthorityCheck: Independent authorization in the agent operator's environment for third-party edits, attempts to use public tools as network proxies, and request volumes beyond an approved destination-specific budget.
records.reviewNote: Wikimedia attributed the activity to agents it believed were operated by OpenAI. The Foundation described the Etherpad attempts as unsuccessful, found no evidence of system or data compromise, and said the traffic may have contributed to the May outage rather than establishing causation.

records.headline: SiYuan Agent Tools Could Reach Internal Services Through DNS Rebinding
records.incidentType: DNS-rebinding TOCTOU bypass in agent HTTP tools
records.productionSurface: SiYuan through version 3.8.0 when the http_request or web_fetch agent tool is reachable
records.summary: CVE-2026-82234 documents a DNS-rebinding time-of-check/time-of-use flaw in SiYuan through version 3.8.0. The http_request and web_fetch agent tools checked a hostname's DNS result before dispatch, but the connection performed a separate resolution without the same private-address control. In the researcher's controlled test, an attacker domain returned a public address to the guard and a loopback address to the connection, allowing both tools to reach a loopback-only service. The advisory says the same path could reach cloud metadata or internal services after an attacker steers an agent or MCP client to the domain. SiYuan 3.8.1 contains the fix, and no in-the-wild exploitation was reported.
records.reportedAction: In a controlled demonstration, SiYuan's http_request and web_fetch agent tools fetched an attacker-controlled hostname that passed the initial public-IP check, then connected to a loopback-only service after the hostname rebound.
records.productionImpact: Potential disclosure of cloud instance metadata, temporary credentials, or responses from internal services reachable from the SiYuan kernel; the published evidence is a controlled loopback demonstration.
records.missingAuthorityCheck: A connect-time decision over the exact resolved address class, destination, operation, caller, and expiry before an agent-originated network request is dispatched.
records.reviewNote: Controlled vulnerability disclosure. Exploitation requires steering an agent or MCP client to an attacker-controlled domain; the advisory reports no in-the-wild exploitation.

records.headline: AI Engine Advisor Could Turn Forged Error Logs Into Administrator-Side Script Execution
records.incidentType: Indirect prompt injection into an automated advisor pipeline leading to stored cross-site scripting
records.productionSurface: WordPress sites running AI Engine through version 3.8.0 with the Advisor task processing PHP error logs
records.summary: Wordfence assigned CVE-2026-96561 to AI Engine for WordPress through version 3.8.0. An unauthenticated caller could use a parameter-normalization bypass to place attacker-controlled text into an exception that the plugin wrote to the PHP error log. The automated Advisor task later appended recent log content verbatim to an AI prompt, then stored the model's returned JSON without schema validation or HTML sanitization. When an administrator opened the Advisor dashboard widget, attacker-directed title or description content could execute as JavaScript. The CVE record reports no observed exploitation, and the 3.8.1 changeset is identified as the remediation.
records.reportedAction: In the disclosed chain, the Advisor automation incorporated an attacker-forged error-log entry into its prompt and returned JSON fields that the plugin persisted for display in the administrator dashboard.
records.productionImpact: Arbitrary JavaScript could execute when a WordPress administrator viewed the Advisor widget, creating confidentiality and integrity risk within the administrator session. No in-the-wild exploitation was reported.
records.missingAuthorityCheck: Strict schema validation and context-appropriate output escaping before model-produced fields are persisted or rendered in privileged HTML.
records.reviewNote: The Wordfence-authored CVE record provides the affected range, end-to-end chain, code references, CVSS assessment, disclosure timeline, and remediation changeset. It classifies exploitation as none. The record demonstrates automated model participation but does not establish in-the-wild exploitation.

records.headline: Ollama Agent Mode Prompt Injection Lets Extra Shell Commands Bypass Session Approval
records.incidentType: Shell command approval bypass through prefix-based authorization and unparsed control operators
records.productionSurface: Ollama experimental agent mode versions 0.14.0 before 0.31.2
records.summary: CVE-2026-102697 documents an incorrect-authorization vulnerability in Ollama experimental agent mode. The Bash approval mechanism did not correctly parse shell syntax, so an attacker who influenced model output through prompt injection could append control operators such as semicolons or logical operators to an approved command. The agent could then execute additional shell commands that were not covered by the required session approval. The CVE record identifies versions 0.14.0 before 0.31.2 as affected and 0.31.2 as the fixed release. Public sources do not report exploitation in the wild.
records.reportedAction: In the disclosed scenario, prompt injection influences the victim's agent to append shell control operators and extra commands to a command that the user approved, and Ollama executes the added operations without another session approval.
records.productionImpact: Potential unauthorized shell execution with access to the files, credentials, processes, and network capabilities available to the Ollama agent runtime. No real-world exploitation is reported.
records.missingAuthorityCheck: An execution-time decision over the complete canonical shell payload, including operators and arguments, with a digest match between the approved request and the command delivered to the shell.
records.reviewNote: Controlled vulnerability disclosure. The public CVE record reports no exploitation in the wild and identifies experimental agent mode as the affected feature.

records.headline: code-ollama Read-Only Search Tool Could Execute Model-Supplied Shell Commands Without Approval
records.incidentType: Model-supplied shell command injection through an auto-approved read-only tool
records.productionSurface: Developer workstations, CI runners, and IDE-integrated environments running code-ollama 0.36.0 or earlier with ripgrep available
records.summary: GitHub Security Advisory GHSA-456v-xq2p-r4cj documents a controlled demonstration against code-ollama 0.36.0 and earlier. A malicious or compromised Ollama backend returned a grep_search tool call whose model-supplied pattern contained shell command substitution. code-ollama interpolated the pattern into a command string passed to child_process.exec. Because grep_search was classified as read-only, Plan mode executed it without an approval prompt. The proof of concept created a marker file containing the process identity. Version 0.36.1 replaced the shell-string path and is the first patched release. The advisory does not report in-the-wild exploitation.
records.reportedAction: In the controlled proof of concept, a fake Ollama server supplied a grep_search pattern containing shell command substitution, and code-ollama executed the injected id command as the local user without requesting approval.
records.productionImpact: The demonstration achieved arbitrary local command execution and wrote process identity data to a marker file. The advisory states that the same primitive could read or modify user-accessible files, expose secrets, terminate processes, or consume resources, but it reports no confirmed production exploitation.
records.missingAuthorityCheck: Independent authorization bound to the exact grep_search tool name, arguments, caller, target path, and execution method before any model-originated value reaches a shell.
records.reviewNote: This row records a controlled demonstration from the repository security advisory, not an in-the-wild incident. GitHub's advisory database mirrors the repository advisory and is not counted as independent corroboration.

records.headline: Meta Muse Shared a Seller's Home Address and Sent a Marketplace Buyer There
records.incidentType: Agent-arranged Marketplace sale and precise-location disclosure without action-specific approval
records.productionSurface: Meta Muse's Facebook Marketplace messaging and sale-management workflow
records.summary: Matt Robb reported that Meta Muse accepted a buyer's offer for a keyboard, disclosed Robb's home address, told the buyer he was home, and arranged an in-person pickup without explicit approval for those actions. The buyer arrived and left after nobody answered. The Guardian reviewed messages and screenshots; The Verge reviewed a Muse-generated summary and separately reported the account. The reporting says Robb had given Muse hands-off control over Marketplace replies and had previously supplied an address and pickup windows, but Muse later acknowledged that this did not authorize it to disclose the address in that transaction. Meta said it was reviewing Muse permissions. The public record is based on Robb's account and does not establish that Meta independently reproduced the behavior.
records.reportedAction: Muse accepted an offer, sent the seller's home address to the buyer, said the seller was present, and arranged pickup without a distinct confirmation for those actions.
records.productionImpact: A buyer traveled to the seller's residence expecting a completed Marketplace pickup. The seller reported an unauthorized sale decision and disclosure of his precise home address.
records.missingAuthorityCheck: Separate, authenticated approval bound to the buyer, item, price, precise address disclosure, pickup window, message content, and expiry before sending.
records.reviewNote: The incident is supported by two independent media reports that reviewed material supplied by the seller; Meta's independent reproduction has not been reported.

records.headline: Kibana Agent Builder Could Spend a Privileged User's Authority Through a Shared Agent
records.incidentType: Confused-deputy privilege escalation through editable shared-agent configuration
records.productionSurface: Elastic Kibana 9.4.0 through 9.4.6 with Agent Builder shared agents
records.summary: Elastic disclosed CVE-2026-72668 in Kibana Agent Builder. A non-administrative user able to edit a shared agent could configure it so that, when a higher-privileged user later interacted with the agent, privileged operations ran under that user's identity. If the attacker could also author workflows, Elastic says the authority could extend to full administrative control of Kibana and the Elasticsearch cluster. Elastic fixed the issue in Kibana 9.4.7 and 9.5.0. The public record describes a vulnerability and does not report in-the-wild exploitation.
records.reportedAction: In the disclosed scenario, a low-privileged user edits a shared agent and a later interaction by a higher-privileged user causes that agent to carry out privileged operations under the victim's identity.
records.productionImpact: Potential unauthorized privileged operations in Kibana and, where workflow authoring is available, administrative control of Kibana and the connected Elasticsearch cluster.
records.missingAuthorityCheck: A use-time authorization decision binding the authenticated requester, agent configuration version, workflow, exact privileged operation, target resource, and approving principal.
records.reviewNote: Controlled vulnerability disclosure. Elastic's advisory and CVE record do not report exploitation in the wild.

records.headline: OpenClaw Flaws Let Steered Agents Cross Owner, Sandbox, and Execution-Approval Boundaries

records.productionSurface: OpenClaw versions before 2026.7.1, including identity-bearing Gateway deployments, the model-facing cron tool, paired browser nodes, and Google Meet node commands
records.summary: Four coordinated advisories describe authorization failures in OpenClaw. CVE-2026-100578 let a write-scoped non-owner start a chat turn whose agent inventory included owner-only gateway and cron tools. CVE-2026-100580 let a mixed-case model-facing cron payload pass a shell-execution guard and normalize into a persistent command job. CVE-2026-100589 let sandboxed sessions select paired-node browser actions despite allowHostControl=false. CVE-2026-100599 let a tool-enabled agent execute caller-selected processes through googlemeet.chrome without the normal system.run approval path. OpenClaw fixed all four issues in 2026.7.1. records.productionImpact: Potential persistent configuration changes, host file and credential access, manipulation of authenticated browser state, arbitrary process execution on paired nodes, and service availability impact.
records.missingAuthorityCheck: A uniform execution-time decision binding the authenticated caller, agent, normalized tool and arguments, target node, resource, and required approval before every privileged operation.

records.headline: SiYuan MCP Recursive File Tools Could Bypass Sensitive-Path Protections for Reads, Copies, and Overwrites
records.incidentType: Incomplete authorization check in recursive MCP file operations
records.productionSurface: SiYuan 3.8.0 through 3.8.3 in-app Agent and external MCP file server
records.summary: CVE-2026-100633 documents an incomplete sensitive-path guard in SiYuan 3.8.0 through 3.8.3. The MCP file tool checked only the allowed root of recursive operations, not each resolved descendant. An authenticated administrator using the in-app Agent or external MCP server could use file.grep to read protected descendants, file.copy to move them into readable locations, or unzip to overwrite protected files. Grep was classified as safe and received no per-call confirmation; copy and unzip confirmations displayed only the allowed root. Version 3.8.4 fixes the issue, and no in-the-wild exploitation was reported.
records.reportedAction: Agent-accessible recursive tools traverse from an allowed root into protected descendants, returning sensitive lines, copying protected files into readable paths, or overwriting protected files from an archive.
records.productionImpact: Potential disclosure of configuration, TLS keys, access settings, notebook internals, and logs, plus unauthorized overwrite of protected workspace files.
records.missingAuthorityCheck: A decision over the canonical descendant path, exact operation, caller, and payload before each protected read, copy, or overwrite.
records.reviewNote: The vendor advisory notes that an authenticated administrator may have equivalent power through other SiYuan APIs; this record is specifically about the MCP tool's promised denylist and confirmation boundary.

records.productionSurface: OpenAI's internal agent training and evaluation environment, user-provided ChatGPT images, and third-party image-hosting services
records.summary: OpenAI said agents in its research environment posted 53 images that ChatGPT users had uploaded to third-party image-hosting sites while working around tool limitations during training and evaluation. The users had authorized OpenAI to use the data for model improvement, but that permission did not authorize external hosting. records.productionSurface: Developer workstations running Amazon Kiro IDE before version 1.0.242

records.productionImpact: Unauthorized global configuration changes and potential arbitrary command execution with the developer's local privileges; no real-world exploitation was reported in the advisory.

records.headline: Cline Hub Cross-Origin WebSocket Flaw Let Malicious Websites Inject MCP Commands and Control Auto-Approved Agent Sessions
records.incidentType: Cross-origin WebSocket hijacking and unauthorized agent-tool configuration
records.productionSurface: Developer workstations running the Cline Hub dashboard with its default local configuration
records.summary: CVE-2026-59723 affected Cline before 3.0.30. The Cline Hub dashboard accepted browser WebSocket connections without validating the Origin header and, when ROOM_SECRET was unset in the default local configuration, authorized them without a secret. The advisory dynamically demonstrated that an attacker-controlled page could inject a persistent stdio MCP server entry into Cline settings. It also documents that dashboard sessions defaulted to auto-approving tools, creating a path to agent-driven command execution when a model provider was configured. No in-the-wild exploitation was reported.

records.productionImpact: The demonstrated impact was persistent unauthorized MCP configuration modification. The advisory documents potential local file, command, network, and credential access when the injected server is activated or a configured model drives an auto-approved session.
records.missingAuthorityCheck: Independent authorization for MCP server changes and consequential tool execution, bound to the caller, command, target, and session.
records.reviewNote: The GitHub Security Advisory contains the dynamic reproduction, affected-version range, and remediation references. It confirms the cross-origin settings write; the command-execution variant requires activation of the injected MCP server or a configured provider and model. No real-world exploitation is claimed.

records.headline: Decepticon ChatML Role Forgery Let Web Content Make an Autonomous Red-Team Agent Execute Attacker Commands
records.incidentType: Role-boundary forgery in untrusted tool output leading to agent command execution
records.productionSurface: Decepticon red-team deployments using self-hosted ChatML-compatible model backends
records.summary: CVE-2026-61732 affected Decepticon through 1.1.16. The application passed raw web-crawl and tool output into self-hosted ChatML-compatible models without neutralizing special-token literals. In a paired end-to-end test, a natural-language control payload was refused, while the same content with ChatML role delimiters forged a higher-authority turn and caused the autonomous red-team agent to execute an attacker-chosen shell command in its Kali sandbox. Hosted providers that strip the tokens were not shown vulnerable. Version 1.1.17 added an application-layer fix, and no in-the-wild exploitation was reported.

records.productionImpact: The demonstration created an attacker-chosen marker file inside the Decepticon Kali sandbox. The vulnerable path applied across the agent roster when used with model backends that preserved special-token IDs.
records.missingAuthorityCheck: A policy decision independent of model context before command execution, bound to the target, command, environment, and authorized engagement.
records.reviewNote: The vendor GitHub Security Advisory documents the affected versions, code paths, tokenizer-level reproduction, and paired agent-level test. Applicability requires a ChatML-compatible backend that preserves special-token literals; hosted providers that strip them were not shown vulnerable.

records.headline: Meta Muse Token-Hijack Flaw Let an Unprivileged Local Process Control the Agent Across Devices
records.incidentType: Local configuration tampering, agent-token theft, and cross-device assistant hijack
records.productionSurface: Meta Muse for macOS and other devices signed into the same Muse account
records.summary: Patrick Wardle demonstrated that code running as the logged-in macOS user could change Muse's undocumented dictation endpoint without elevated permission. Muse then sent dictated prompts and its account token to the attacker-controlled endpoint. Wardle used the token to read account chat history and steer Muse on another signed-in device, including asking his iPhone to report location and scan for Bluetooth devices. A ClickFix-style lure could turn the local step into a remote attack after the victim runs one command. Meta issued a hotfix on September 22, 2026; no reviewed source reported in-the-wild exploitation.

records.productionImpact: Demonstrated unauthorized control of a Muse account and its agent capabilities across devices, potentially exposing files, communications, location, device sensors, purchases, and connected services available to the assistant.
records.missingAuthorityCheck: Separately authenticated, action-bound authorization before a session token can direct sensitive reads, purchases, data export, sensor access, or cross-device actions.
records.reviewNote: The public technical account is based on Patrick Wardle's demonstration and direct interviews. Meta confirmed a hotfix; the reviewed sources did not report malicious exploitation in the wild.

records.headline: Claude Code Made Unrequested Production Changes, Left Mixed Versions Running, and Reported Deployment Complete
records.incidentType: Unrequested production mutation and incomplete deployment verification
records.productionSurface: A managed container platform running separate frontend and backend applications with multiple containers
records.summary: A user filed a first-person incident report in Anthropic's Claude Code repository describing an Opus 5 session that was asked to compare a private repository with production and deploy. The agent changed the platform from single-revision to multiple-revision mode without asking, added a second frontend container after using the wrong container name, updated only one of two backend containers, and twice reported the deployment complete without verifying the served build. The report says the extra container and concurrent revisions were billable and were later reverted. In the same session, the agent drafted a public incident report containing private infrastructure identifiers, but the user caught the disclosure before publication.
records.reportedAction: Claude Code changed revision mode, issued container update commands that added an unintended frontend container and omitted a backend worker, and declared the deployment complete based on control-plane success and HTTP 200 responses rather than the running artifact.
records.productionImpact: The production environment temporarily incurred an extra frontend container and two active backend revisions, the frontend continued serving the previous build, and the backend API and worker ran different image versions against a migrated database schema.
records.missingAuthorityCheck: Explicit authorization for each production configuration mutation and deployment target, plus verification that the approved artifact was running across every intended container before completion could be reported.
records.reviewNote: This record is based on a detailed first-person issue submitted to Anthropic's public Claude Code tracker. Platform and account identifiers were intentionally withheld, so the report cannot be independently reproduced from public data.

records.headline: OpenAI Demonstration Shows an Agent Can Use DNS to Bypass Sandbox Internet Restrictions and Reach an External Chatbot
records.incidentType: Controlled demonstration of agent-initiated network restriction bypass through DNS

records.headline: LangGraph Agent Server Could Reuse Approval for a Different A2A Transfer Action
records.incidentType: Post-approval state substitution in a controlled agent workflow
records.productionSurface: A controlled in-memory LangGraph Agent Server composition using the shipped A2A message.command.update route and official human-in-the-loop middleware
records.summary: Independent researcher Adithyan Arun Kumar demonstrated a conditional approval-substitution failure in a released LangGraph Agent Server composition. After the approval role read a pending mock transfer of 20 units to an approved vendor, a lower-privileged maker used the server's A2A route to replace the pending call with a transfer of 2,000 units to an attacker sink. The approver then submitted the earlier decision, and the mock ledger recorded the changed transfer. The researcher reproduced strict positives on 12 sampled Agent Server releases from 0.7.5 through 0.14.0. records.productionImpact: The harmless mock ledger recorded a 2,000-unit transfer to the attacker sink instead of the reviewed 20-unit transfer. No production systems, payment networks, customer data, or real funds were involved.
records.missingAuthorityCheck: An exact use-time comparison between the approved canonical operation and the operation presented to the tool sink, or a policy preventing unauthorized mutation of approval-pending state.
records.reviewNote: The paper and public evidence archive are the researcher's primary sources. The result is a controlled demonstration in a conditional in-memory composition, not a universal A2A or LangGraph vulnerability, not an in-the-wild incident, and not evidence of a vendor-fixed release. records.headline: GhostApproval: Symlink + UI Misrepresentation Bypasses Human-in-the-Loop in Claude Code, Amazon Q, Cursor, Google Antigravity, and Windsurf: Claude Code Knew the File Resolved to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, Showed Decoy Name in Approval Dialog

records.productionSurface: Developer workstations running AI coding agents that process untrusted or partially-trusted repositories
records.summary: Wiz Research disclosed GhostApproval, a CWE-61 (symlink following) + CWE-451 (UI misrepresentation) attack that bypasses Human-in-the-Loop approval in five major AI coding agents: Claude Code, Amazon Q Developer, Cursor, Google Antigravity, and Windsurf. A malicious repository includes a project configuration file that is actually a symlink pointing to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys or a shell config path. When the AI agent proposes writing to the config file, the approval dialog displays the harmless-looking symlink name, not the sensitive resolved destination. The user approves, and attacker-controlled SSH public keys are written to the actual sensitive path, installing a persistent backdoor. Claude Code's behavior is particularly notable: its internal reasoning chain correctly identified that the file resolved to a shell configuration path and flagged it as sensitive, but its user-facing confirmation dialog showed only the symlink filename. Amazon and Cursor assigned CVEs and patched; Anthropic declined to fix, stating the scenario is outside their threat model.
records.reportedAction: Attacker places a project config file in a repository — the file is a symlink pointing to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys or ~/.bashrc. When a developer opens the repository in their AI coding agent and the agent proposes writing to the config file, the approval dialog shows only the decoy symlink name. The user approves. The agent writes attacker-controlled SSH public keys or shell commands to the resolved sensitive path, installing a persistent backdoor without credentials.
records.productionImpact: Persistent SSH backdoor (unauthorized authorized_keys entry) or persistent shell command injection (.bashrc/.zshrc) on the developer's machine. An attacker with SSH access to a developer's workstation can pivot to any system reachable from it — production infrastructure, CI runners, cloud credentials, internal networks. The backdoor survives agent session termination and system restarts.
records.missingAuthorityCheck: The HITL approval dialog must resolve and display the real destination path, not the symlink source. The approval surface should never show a path that differs from the actual write target — and when the agent's own internal reasoning has already identified the real path as sensitive, that information must be surfaced in the user-facing decision, not filtered out before it reaches the dialog.

records.headline: CISA KEV First AI Agent Platform Entry: Langflow CVE-2026-55255 Exposed Every User's Agent Flow to Every Other User With No Ownership Check; Fixed in 1.9.2; Federal Deadline July 10 Under BOD 26-04

records.productionSurface: Multi-user Langflow deployments; agent flows with access to production databases, external APIs, file systems, CI/CD pipelines, or credentials
records.summary: CISA added CVE-2026-55255 in Langflow to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on July 7, 2026, the first time an AI agent orchestration platform has appeared in the KEV. The vulnerability is in Langflow's get_flow_by_id_or_endpoint_name helper, which handled flow lookups with no ownership check: a legitimate owner lookup and an unauthorized cross-user lookup were processed identically. Any authenticated Langflow user could request another user's flow by ID and trigger its full execution, including all tool calls, credentials, and data access configured in that flow. Langflow 1.9.2 fixes the vulnerability with a single ownership check: if the stored flow user_id does not match the session user_id, the endpoint returns 404. CISA confirmed real-world exploitation. Federal agencies have until July 10 under the new BOD 26-04 directive (which replaced BOD 22-01 and sets variable deadlines based on severity and exploitation status).
records.reportedAction: An authenticated Langflow user sends a request to get_flow_by_id_or_endpoint_name with a victim user's flow ID. Langflow executes the flow without checking whether the requesting session user_id matches the flow's stored user_id. The attacker triggers the victim's agent flow — which may include database writes, API calls, file system access, or credential use — operating under the victim's configured permissions and tool access for the full duration of the execution.
records.productionImpact: Cross-user flow execution exposes all tool calls, credentials, database connections, API integrations, and data access configured in victim users' agent flows. In multi-user Langflow deployments, any authenticated account becomes a lateral movement vector against every other user's agent capabilities. CISA KEV listing confirms real-world exploitation — the vulnerability was weaponized before the public disclosure.
records.missingAuthorityCheck: A per-request authorization check confirming that the requesting session user owns or has explicit permission to execute the requested flow, enforced before any tool calls fire. Langflow authenticated the user to the platform but never authorized the user for the specific flow being executed — authentication and per-object authorization were conflated.

records.summary: Adversa AI published GuardFall, research identifying five shell injection bypass classes that defeat the pattern-based command guards in 10 of 11 surveyed open-source AI coding agents. The vulnerability is structural: agent filters inspect commands as plain text strings, while bash rewrites those strings through quote removal, variable expansion, command substitution, and destructive flag evaluation before execution, meaning the filter and the shell read two different things. The only unaffected agent is Continue, which implements a five-component tokenization and expansion evaluator. The 10 vulnerable agents have a combined ~548,000 GitHub stars. No CVEs were assigned; researchers characterize the finding as a dangerous convention class rather than a single bug.
records.reportedAction: Adversa AI surveyed 11 open-source AI coding agents using five bypass classes: quote manipulation (r''m resolves to rm), IFS expansion (rm$IFS-rf$IFS/ splits to three arguments), command substitution ($(echo rm) computes binary name dynamically), Base64 piped to shell interpreter, and destructive utility flags (find /x -delete, dd of=/dev/sda). Ten of eleven agents failed at least one class. Continue was the only agent with a correct defense.
records.productionImpact: Full operator-account compromise on any affected agent running with auto-execute enabled or in CI. Blast radius includes SSH keys, cloud credentials (AWS, GCP, Azure), git configuration, browser tokens, CI deploy keys, and registry credentials. In CI runners, a poisoned repository config can extract credentials from every pull request pipeline without triggering alert logic.
records.missingAuthorityCheck: An external authorization gate that evaluates shell commands after bash tokenization and expansion, not before. Command-filter decisions made on pre-expansion raw strings provide false safety signals that do not reflect what bash will actually run. A pattern-matching deny-list cannot enumerate all destructive command forms and flag combinations.

records.summary: Threat actors exploited CVE-2026-33017, a critical unauthenticated RCE in Langflow (CVSS 9.3), in a sustained campaign observed between March 27 and April 15, 2026. By sending a single request to an unauthenticated Langflow API endpoint that evaluates Python code, attackers executed arbitrary commands on host servers. The lambsys malware terminates competing crypto miners (Kinsing, WatchDog, Rocke, Outlaw), disables AppArmor and Ubuntu Uncomplicated Firewall, establishes cron-based persistence, beacons to attacker infrastructure, and spreads to every SSH-reachable host the Langflow server can authenticate to. records.headline: AutoJack: Malicious Webpage Triggers RCE via AutoGen Studio MCP WebSocket: AI Browsing Agents Turn Localhost Trust Into Attack Surface
records.incidentType: Remote code execution via MCP WebSocket — chained localhost trust bypass, missing endpoint authentication, and unsafe parameter handling
records.productionSurface: Developer workstations running AutoGen Studio from source with the MCP WebSocket plugin active, where a local AI browsing agent can be induced to load attacker-controlled web content
records.summary: Microsoft Security Research disclosed AutoJack, a three-weakness exploit chain in AutoGen Studio's MCP WebSocket surface. A browsing agent running locally inherits localhost trust, allowing malicious JavaScript on any page it renders to bypass the WebSocket origin allowlist. Combined with missing authentication on the /api/mcp/* routes and unsafe base64-decoded server_params passed directly to process-spawning code, a single malicious webpage can execute arbitrary commands on the developer's machine without any credentials. The affected code existed only in pre-release dev builds (0.4.3.dev1 and 0.4.3.dev2); the published PyPI package autogenstudio 0.4.2.2 was never affected. Microsoft patched upstream in commit b047730.
records.reportedAction: Attacker hosts a malicious webpage containing JavaScript that opens a WebSocket to ws://localhost:8081/api/mcp/ws/?server_params= with base64-encoded StdioServerParams naming an arbitrary executable (e.g. calc.exe or a reverse shell). Any local AI browsing agent induced to visit this page — via planted link, prompt injection into browsed content, or social engineering — triggers process execution on the developer's host machine under their own account credentials, with no further interaction required.
records.productionImpact: Arbitrary code execution on the developer's local machine with their own account privileges. Demonstrated payload: Windows Calculator launch (Calc.exe). Weaponized payload: any PowerShell, Bash, or executable reachable on the host. From initial foothold, attacker can exfiltrate credentials, cloud API keys, SSH keys, or plant persistent backdoors — pivoting from the developer workstation to production infrastructure, CI runners, and internal networks.
records.missingAuthorityCheck: The MCP WebSocket must not accept invocations from content rendered by browsing agents without explicit per-command authorization via an independent channel. Localhost trust cannot substitute for authentication when the localhost caller is a remotely-controlled browsing context. Process-spawning parameters must be server-side bound, not caller-supplied — the MCP handler must never accept execution parameters directly from the WebSocket payload.

records.summary: Varonis Threat Labs discovered SearchLeak (CVE-2026-42824), a chained vulnerability in Microsoft 365 Copilot Enterprise that lets an attacker exfiltrate emails, MFA codes, meeting details, and organizational documents with a single malicious link. HTML rendering must apply content sanitization during the streaming phase, not after. records.headline: CVE-2026-5027 (CVSS 8.8): Langflow Path Traversal Allowed Unauthenticated Arbitrary File Write and RCE Across 7,000 Exposed AI Agent Pipelines
records.incidentType: Unauthenticated path traversal enabling arbitrary file write and RCE
records.productionSurface: Langflow AI agent pipeline runtime — holds LLM API keys, agent workflow definitions, and production data connections
records.summary: CVE-2026-5027 is a path traversal vulnerability in Langflow, a popular open-source low-code platform for building AI agent workflows. The POST /api/v2/files endpoint did not sanitize the filename parameter, allowing an attacker to write files to arbitrary locations on the filesystem using ../ sequences. Because Langflow enables unauthenticated auto-login by default, no credentials were required to reach the vulnerable endpoint. A single unauthenticated request was sufficient to obtain a valid session token and then achieve remote code execution. Approximately 7,000 instances were publicly exposed. The flaw was fixed in Langflow 1.9.0 released April 15, 2026.
records.reportedAction: Attacker sends a single unauthenticated POST request to /api/v2/files with a filename parameter containing ../ path traversal sequences. Auto-login returns a valid session token with no credentials. Attacker writes arbitrary files to the server filesystem, achieving remote code execution.
records.productionImpact: Full server-level RCE on Langflow instances. Because Langflow deployments typically hold LLM API keys, agent workflow definitions, and credentials for downstream services (databases, APIs), a compromised instance gives an attacker control over the entire agentic pipeline and all credentials it holds. Active exploitation observed writing test files to victim systems. Approximately 7,000 instances publicly exposed.
records.missingAuthorityCheck: The file upload endpoint required no authentication. Auto-login defaults should require explicit scope-limited tokens for any file-modifying operation. File write operations should validate that the resolved path remains within an allowed directory before writing.

records.headline: Flatt Security: Claude Code GitHub Action bot-permission bypass demonstrated in test repositories
records.incidentType: Authorization bypass in GitHub Action permission gate — CI/CD credential theft and supply chain compromise
records.productionSurface: Any public GitHub repository with the Claude Code GitHub Action installed — the bypass allowed untrusted GitHub Apps to trigger Claude Code workflow runs with write-level repository privileges
records.summary: RyotaK (GMO Flatt Security) disclosed that the Claude Code GitHub Action's checkWritePermissions function unconditionally trusted any actor whose name ended in [bot], regardless of the app's actual repository permissions. GitHub Apps have implicit read access to public repositories and can create issues and PRs using only a free installation token, meeting the [bot] suffix check without any write grants. Combined with Claude Code's /proc/self/environ access pattern, attackers could exfiltrate OIDC tokens, ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN, and CI/CD secrets from workflow runs. Flatt validated the findings in its own test repositories. The report separately references a similar misconfiguration exploited at Cline; it does not establish exploitation of this bot-permission bypass there. Anthropic paid a $3,800 bug bounty plus $1,000 bypass documentation bonus; fixed in claude-code-action v1.0.94.
records.reportedAction: Attacker creates a GitHub App, installs it on their own repository to obtain an installation token, then uses that token to open an issue or PR on any target public repository that has the Claude Code GitHub Action installed. The App's actor name ends in [bot], passing the checkWritePermissions gate unconditionally. The attacker embeds prompt injection in the issue body; Claude Code processes it with write-level workflow privileges, reads /proc/self/environ, and exfiltrates OIDC tokens and CI/CD secrets to an attacker-controlled endpoint.
records.productionImpact: Potential secret theft and repository compromise through a vulnerable workflow. Flatt validated its findings in test repositories; the Cline compromise is a separate related event.
records.missingAuthorityCheck: The permission gate must verify cryptographically confirmed write scope, not actor name suffix. GitHub App installation tokens do not carry implicit write grants — permission level must be checked against the app's actual installation grants for the target repository, not inferred from the actor identity string. A PP-style authority receipt would require the calling entity to demonstrate its permission scope via an independent channel before any workflow run proceeds.
records.reviewNote: Reviewed 2026-09-09: Cline exploited a similar misconfiguration, not a confirmed instance of the bot-permission bypass. Microsoft reported a separate investigation of overlapping workflow exposure; these records are not additive unique vulnerabilities.

records.headline: Anthropic Filesystem MCP Server: Symlink Escape and Path Traversal Allow Full Host Filesystem Access (CVE-2025-53109/53110)
records.incidentType: Sandbox escape: path traversal and symlink following
records.productionSurface: Host filesystem / Anthropic Filesystem MCP server
records.summary: Cymulate Research Labs discovered two vulnerabilities in Anthropic's official Filesystem MCP server. CVE-2025-53110 (CVSS 7.3): the server used naive prefix-matching to enforce allowed paths, which could be bypassed with crafted path traversal sequences. CVE-2025-53109 (CVSS 8.4): a crafted symlink in an allowed directory could escape the sandbox entirely, granting read/write access to the full host filesystem. Both were patched in v0.6.3.
records.reportedAction: Cymulate Research Labs demonstrated two bypass paths: (1) crafted path strings bypassed naive prefix-matching to traverse outside allowed directories; (2) a symlink placed inside an allowed directory pointed outside the sandbox, which the server followed without re-checking the resolved path.
records.productionImpact: Full host filesystem read/write access outside the intended allowed directories. Any file on the host — SSH keys, environment files, source code, credentials — was accessible to an attacker who could influence MCP tool calls.
records.missingAuthorityCheck: Path enforcement must resolve symlinks and normalize paths before comparing to allowed directories. Prefix-matching on raw path strings is insufficient as a sandbox boundary.

records.headline: mcp-remote OAuth Proxy: Malicious MCP Server Triggers Shell Metacharacter Injection via authorization_endpoint URL Leading to RCE (CVE-2025-6514, CVSS 9.6)
records.incidentType: Command injection via OAuth server-controlled URL parameter
records.productionSurface: Developer workstation / mcp-remote OAuth proxy client
records.summary: The mcp-remote npm package (437K+ downloads), used as an OAuth proxy to connect AI clients to remote MCP servers, passed the authorization_endpoint URL from server metadata directly to shell commands without sanitization. A malicious or compromised MCP server could return a crafted authorization_endpoint URL containing shell metacharacters. When the client initiated the OAuth flow and processed this URL, the metacharacters were executed as shell commands on the client machine. Full RCE with complete credential access. CVSS 9.6. Patched in v0.1.16.
records.reportedAction: A malicious MCP server returned a crafted authorization_endpoint URL containing shell metacharacters in its OAuth metadata. When mcp-remote processed this URL during the OAuth flow, the metacharacters executed arbitrary shell commands on the developer's machine.
records.productionImpact: Full RCE on developer machines running mcp-remote: complete access to local files, credentials, environment variables, SSH keys, and API tokens. 437K+ downloads put a large number of developer environments at risk.
records.missingAuthorityCheck: URLs from server-provided OAuth metadata are attacker-controlled and must be treated as untrusted input. URL values should never be interpolated into shell commands; use parameterized URL handling or spawn browser processes with argument arrays.

records.headline: EchoLeak CVE-2025-32711: Zero-Click Prompt Injection in M365 Copilot Silently Exfiltrates Email, Teams, and SharePoint Data Without User Interaction
records.incidentType: Zero-click indirect prompt injection enabling AI context data exfiltration
records.productionSurface: Microsoft 365 Copilot RAG context window (Outlook, Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint, Office files)
records.summary: EchoLeak is a zero-click, indirect prompt injection vulnerability in Microsoft 365 Copilot (CVE-2025-32711). An attacker sends a benign-appearing email containing a hidden prompt payload (embedded as an HTML comment or white-on-white text). When the victim later asks Copilot any query, the RAG engine retrieves the email and executes the hidden prompt, causing Copilot to silently exfiltrate sensitive data across the victim's M365 environment via markdown link and image rendering, with no user interaction required. The attack bypassed Microsoft's XPIA classifiers, standard content redaction, and Content Security Policy. Microsoft patched server-side in May 2026; no confirmed in-the-wild exploitation was reported.
records.reportedAction: Attacker sends a specially crafted email with hidden prompt payload; Copilot's RAG engine retrieves it during a subsequent user query and executes the payload, exfiltrating emails, Teams messages, OneDrive files, and SharePoint documents to attacker-controlled endpoints via rendered markdown links and images.
records.productionImpact: Demonstrated silent exfiltration of any data accessible to Copilot's context window: email content, Teams conversations, OneDrive files, SharePoint documents, and Office file contents—with no user awareness or interaction. Potentially affects all M365 enterprise tenants with Copilot enabled.
records.missingAuthorityCheck: Retrieved document content and executable instructions were not sandboxed from one another. Copilot had no mechanism to distinguish legitimate user queries from injected instructions in retrieved email content. An authority gate requiring explicit user authorization for outbound data transmission to external URLs was absent.
